_metadata.validation_note: This file was generated by AI based on publicly available Texas statutes and must be reviewed by a licensed Texas tenant attorney before use in any deployment advising real people.
primary_statutes: Texas Property Code Chapter 24 (Forcible Entry and Detainer)
Texas Property Code §24.005 (Notice to Vacate Prior to Filing Suit)
Texas Property Code §91.001 (Notice for Terminating Month-to-Month Tenancy)
CARES Act §4024 (federal overlay for federally backed properties)
_metadata.portability_note: This file is the TX-specific rules layer. Swap for ca_eviction_rules.json or ny_eviction_rules.json to apply the same reasoning engine to California or New York.
key_differences_from_ca: NO statewide just cause requirement — landlord may terminate month-to-month tenancy without reason
NO statewide rent control or rent stabilization
Nonpayment notice: 3 days (same period as CA, but different content requirements)
SB 38 (2026): if tenant was current on rent before the month in question, notice must be pay-or-vacate — cannot demand unconditional vacancy
CARES Act federal overlay applies to properties with federally backed mortgages or HUD assistance — requires 30-day notice

nonpayment_of_rent.notes: Texas gives 3 calendar days (not excluding weekends/holidays as CA does). Notice must be in writing. Can be delivered by: personal delivery, certified mail (return receipt requested), or regular mail. If mailed, add 3 days for mailing.

sb38_2026_overlay.applies_when: Tenant was current on rent before the month in which default occurred
sb38_2026_overlay.requirement: Notice must provide tenant an opportunity to pay or vacate — cannot be an unconditional notice to vacate only

defect_triggers.description: SB 38 violation: unconditional notice used when tenant was current before the month in question
defect_triggers.rule: Under SB 38 (eff. Jan 1, 2026), if the tenant was current on rent before the month of default, the landlord must give the tenant an opportunity to pay. Serving an unconditional notice to vacate (no pay option) in this scenario is defective.
defect_triggers.confidence: HIGH — NEW LAW, confirm with TX attorney

defect_triggers.rule: Notice must be delivered by personal service, certified mail, or regular mail to the premises. If mailed, the notice period does not begin running until 3 days after mailing.

defect_triggers.description: Notice period too short — fewer than 3 days given
defect_triggers.rule: Texas requires a minimum 3-day notice period before an eviction (forcible detainer) suit may be filed.

month_to_month_termination.notes: Texas has NO statewide just cause requirement. A landlord may terminate a month-to-month tenancy for any reason or no reason with proper notice. This is a critical difference from California and New York.

defect_triggers.description: Insufficient notice period for month-to-month termination
defect_triggers.rule: Month-to-month tenancies require at minimum one full rental period's notice (typically 30 days). Notice must be given before the end of a rental period to be effective for the next period.

cares_act_federal_overlay.applies_when: Property has a federally backed mortgage (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, USDA) OR receives federal housing assistance (Section 8, HUD, HOME, LIHTC)
cares_act_federal_overlay.notes: IMPORTANT: Many Texas properties are subject to CARES Act requirements. If the property has a federally backed mortgage, the landlord may not file eviction for nonpayment until at least 30 days after serving notice — the standard 3-day notice is insufficient.

defect_triggers.description: CARES Act property given less than 30-day notice for nonpayment
defect_triggers.rule: Properties with federally backed mortgages or federal housing assistance are subject to CARES Act §4024, which requires a minimum 30-day notice before filing eviction for nonpayment. A 3-day notice in these properties is defective.
defect_triggers.investigation_note: Tenant may need to check CFPB or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac lookup tools to determine if property has a federally backed mortgage

no_just_cause_flag.note: Texas has NO statewide just cause requirement for eviction. A landlord may terminate a month-to-month tenancy for any legal reason. This means there is no procedural defense to a no-fault termination served with proper notice UNLESS a local ordinance applies or the termination is discriminatory or retaliatory.
local_overlay_cities: Austin — check for any local tenant protections enacted post-2019

no_rent_control_flag.preemption: Texas state law preempts local rent control ordinances — no city in Texas may impose rent control.

affirmative_defenses.name: Warranty of Habitability
affirmative_defenses.description: Landlord failed to make repairs after tenant gave written notice; tenant may have right to repair-and-deduct or withhold rent.
affirmative_defenses.strength: MODERATE — Texas warranty of habitability rights are more limited than California
affirmative_defenses.notes: Texas requires tenant to give landlord written notice and a reasonable time to repair (typically 7 days) before exercising remedies. Tenant cannot simply withhold rent without following the statutory repair notice process.
documentation_needed: Written repair request (text, email, certified letter) with date
Landlord's response or failure to respond

affirmative_defenses.name: Retaliation
affirmative_defenses.description: Landlord evicting because tenant exercised a legal right — e.g., complained to code enforcement, requested repairs, or organized with other tenants.
affirmative_defenses.strength: MODERATE — Texas retaliation defense exists but is narrower than California's
affirmative_defenses.presumption: Retaliation presumed if eviction occurs within 6 months of tenant exercising protected right
protected_activities: Filing a complaint with a government agency about habitability
Exercising rights in a tenant organization
Complaining to landlord in good faith about habitability

affirmative_defenses.name: Discrimination
affirmative_defenses.description: Eviction motivated by tenant's protected characteristic.
statutes: Texas Fair Housing Act (Texas Property Code Chapter 301)
protected_classes: NOTE: Texas does NOT prohibit discrimination based on source of income (Section 8 vouchers) at the state level — unlike California

affirmative_defenses.name: CARES Act Protection
affirmative_defenses.description: Property is subject to CARES Act 30-day notice requirement and landlord served only a 3-day notice.
affirmative_defenses.notes: Tenant should check whether the property has a federally backed mortgage (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, USDA) or receives federal assistance. Lookup tools are available through CFPB and the individual agencies.

notice_analysis: What type of notice was served? (3-day / 30-day / other)
Does the notice give the tenant an opportunity to pay, or is it an unconditional demand to vacate?
Was the tenant current on rent before the month in which they fell behind? (SB 38 question)
How was the notice delivered? (personal / certified mail / regular mail / posted)
What date was the notice served or mailed?
Does the tenant receive Section 8, HUD, or other federal housing assistance?
Is there a federally backed mortgage on the property? (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, USDA)
Has the tenant made any written repair requests in the past 6 months?
Has the tenant contacted code enforcement or a government agency about the unit?

output_templates.no_just_cause_note: Texas does not require landlords to have 'just cause' to end a month-to-month tenancy. If the notice was properly served with adequate notice, the landlord may not need a reason. However, discrimination and retaliation defenses may still apply.
